title: External ops clarification: fallback sequence and data preservation (draft customer update)
content:
Purpose and intended audience:
This doc is a draft external update intended for customers who observed degraded inference throughput on 2025-07-13. It contains: a concise status-page style blurb we can post immediately, a short customer-facing postmortem summary suitable for emailed status updates, and an FAQ about fallback behavior and data preservation. Keep tone calm and engineering-forward; avoid deep internal jargon.

Status page blurb (one-line + details):
- ONE LINE: Partial throughput degradation resolved — automatic fallback sequence reduced availability for some single-region Dedicated pools between 2025-07-13 03:42–04:18 UTC.
- DETAILS (for staging on status page): Impact: From ~03:42–04:18 UTC, a subset of requests routed to Dedicated pools experienced elevated queuing and increased tail latency. Customer-facing symptoms: occasional 502/504 responses and higher than normal per-request latency for models with long context windows (>2k tokens).
- Scope: ~4% of dedicated capacity across eu-west and us-central regions; no known request payload corruption or data loss.
- Current status: Resolved. We reverted the fallback automation and applied a patch to the routing policy. All routes have returned to normal throughput and latency baselines as of 04:18 UTC.
- Next updates: Follow-up summary (RCA + customer mitigations) will be published within 72 hours.

Short customer-facing postmortem (suitable for email or support portal):
Summary: On 2025-07-13 at ~03:42 UTC an automated fallback sequence intended to protect latency SLOs triggered incorrectly for a subset of Dedicated pools operating at high token-rate for long-context models. The fallback caused traffic redirection to lower-capacity model variants and temporary request throttling which manifested as elevated latency and a small number of 5xx errors for some customers. There was no exposure of customer data and no loss of stored inputs or outputs.
Root cause (high level): A combination of (a) an earlier routing-policy change that relaxed capacity checks, (b) a spike in long-context burst traffic from a customer in eu-west, and (c) a stale health-check threshold caused the system to classify healthy nodes as "degraded." This classification triggered the fallback sequencer which gradually moved traffic to variants that did not have sufficient burst headroom, increasing queueing.
Mitigations we executed (immediate):
- Rolled back the routing-policy change to restore strict capacity prechecks (03:50 UTC).
- Temporarily paused the fallback automation for affected tenant tiers while we validated node health (03:55 UTC).
- Applied a routing hotfix tightening health-check sensitivity and increased allowed burst capacity for model-variant pools (04:05 UTC).
- Monitored for 30 minutes and declared resolution at 04:18 UTC.
What customers should know:
- Data integrity: No requests were dropped permanently; for affected requests we either served a degraded-but-valid response (from variant model) or returned 5xx transient error which can be retried. No stored embeddings, logs, or payloads were truncated or lost.
- Recommended immediate action: If you saw 5xxs during the window, please retry requests; implement exponential backoff for burst traffic. If you rely on strict latency SLOs for long-context calls, contact your account team to discuss pinning to dedicated capacity or temporarily increasing burst reservations.

Short FAQ / Troubleshooting guidance for customers:
Q: Did you lose any customer data or logs?
A: No. All telemetry and request/response logs are intact. We have validated storage consistency for embeddings and outputs.

Q: Why did fallback make things worse for some customers?
A: The fallback sequencer assumes target variants have spare headroom. In this incident, traffic shifted to variants that were already near capacity for long-context workloads, which increased queueing and tail latency. We've updated the variant selection heuristic to prefer variants with proven burst headroom for long-context token distributions.

Q: Will Redwood offer SLA credits?
A: We are evaluating the impact relative to customer SLAs. The follow-up postmortem will include a summary of affected tenants and any proposed crediting. If you believe your service-level obligations were materially impacted, open a support ticket with the incident reference (JIRA-INC-2025-0721) and your account team will prioritize review.

Q: What changes are you making to prevent recurrence?
A: Short-term (this week): revert risky routing changes to a canary-only rollout, harden health-check thresholds, and add an interlock that prevents fallback if destination variant utilization > 70%. Medium-term (30–90 days): enhanced simulation of fallback sequences with historical traffic profiles, autoscaler improvements to better anticipate long-context bursts, and expanded observability that correlates token-length distributions with variant capacity.

Internal notes / items to resolve before final publish (TODOs):
- Confirm list of affected customer IDs and whether any enterprise contracts require immediate outreach (owner: Priya Patel).
- Draft the final postmortem for the public status page with an anonymized impact table (owner: Maya Chen + engineering liaison Jared Kim).
- Validate PR 4125 does not affect unrelated routing flows (owner: Evelyn Brooks).
- Decide on SLA credit methodology and approvals (owner: Finance & Legal).

Suggested 72-hour public postmortem outline (for status page):
1) Impact summary (what happened, who was affected)
2) Timeline of events with timestamps in UTC and customer local offsets
3) Root cause (non-technical summary + detailed appendix for customers who want deeper info)
4) Immediate mitigations and what customers should do now
5) Long-term fixes and ETA
6) Contact and escalation path (support link + account rep contact)

Tone/wording guidance for final copy:
- Avoid naming internal feature flags or very detailed internal runbooks on the public page.
- Be explicit about impact and action customers should take.
- Reassure on data safety early in the message.
- Include clear next steps and timelines.

Draft email blurb for account teams (short):
Subject: Update: Resolved degraded throughput for some Dedicated pools (2025-07-13)
Hi <Customer Name>,
We wanted to let you know about a transient throughput degradation that affected some Dedicated capacity between 03:42–04:18 UTC on 2025-07-13. We have resolved the issue; there was no data loss. If you experienced increased latency or transient errors, please retry requests and reach out to your account team for assistance. We will publish a detailed follow-up postmortem within 72 hours.
Thanks,
The Redwood Ops Team

Notes to self: keep final public language to 3–4 short paragraphs + 1 FAQ section. Coordinate publication time with SRE and Legal to ensure metrics and impacted-tenants list are approved.

--- end of draft ---
